transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is... I’ve been noticing I don’t always take in what people are saying, even when I’m looking right at them. Like at the museum—there’s this art walk they’re planning, and someone will be talking to me about where people should go next, or what’s happening, and I’ll be nodding along, but then I realize I missed the middle part. Then I have to ask them to run it by me again.

It’s a little embarrassing, honestly, because I’m not trying to ignore anyone.
When this happens, does it feel like you hear the words clearly but they don’t register?

Yeah, that’s pretty much it. I hear them talking, and I’m looking right at them, but then somewhere in the middle it’s like it just didn’t stick. Like at the museum, when they’re explaining the next art walk—where folks are supposed to go or what’s happening next—I’ll be nodding, and then I realize I missed part of it and have to ask them to say it again.

It’s not that I’m trying to tune them out. It’s just… it doesn’t always register.
Do you often have trouble staying focused in other situations too, not just when people are talking to you?

Yeah, I think so. Like if I sit down with a gallery packet or some notes, I’ll start out okay, you know, like I’m reading it and following along. But then after a few minutes my eyes are still going over the page, and my mind is somewhere else entirely.

Sometimes I’ll get to the bottom and realize I don’t really know what I just read, so I have to go back over the same part again. It’s funny, because some of those packets are pretty straightforward, and they remind me of the little handouts they used to give at community events—anyway, yeah, it happens with reading things too, not just when someone’s talking.
Did you have problems like this with paying attention when you were a child?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, going way back, even in grade school my report cards had little comments like “daydreams” or “needs reminders to finish work.” I remember my mother sitting next to me while I did homework, just to kind of keep me moving along—this was before I was twelve, I’m pretty sure.

Funny thing is, I can still picture the kitchen table more than the homework itself… but yes, it was there when I was a kid too.
Have you been feeling down or depressed مؤخراً?

I’m not sure I’d say depressed, exactly. I mean, I have my days where I’m a little off or quiet, but… nothing that’s really jumped out at me recently.

Sometimes the weather changes and I get kind of slowed down—my neighbor says that happens to him too—but I don’t know if that’s what you mean. I haven’t really noticed feeling down in a big way.
Do you often feel anxious or worried?

I don’t know… I wouldn’t say I’m especially anxious. I mean, I worry about regular things, like appointments or whether I left something where I can find it again, but I don’t think I’m sitting around feeling worried all the time.

Sometimes if there’s a lot going on, I get a little keyed up, but then again, that might just be normal. My sister used to make lists for everything—she’d have one for groceries, one for errands, even one for phone calls—and I always thought maybe I should do that more. But no, I haven’t really noticed a big anxiety problem.
When people speak, do you ever feel like you can hear the sound of their voice but the words themselves are hard to make out?

Hmm… I’m not sure. I mean, sometimes if there’s background noise, like the TV is on or we’re in a restaurant, I might miss what someone said and ask them to repeat it. But I don’t know if that’s the words being hard to make out or just me not catching it.

My wife used to say I’d nod along and then not know what she asked me to do—but that’s a different thing, I guess. So… no, I haven’t really noticed it as a problem with hearing the voice but not the words.
Do these attention lapses cause problems for you in daily life, like at work, at home, or in relationships?

Yeah… I guess they do, a bit. Not like everything’s falling apart, but with the museum group—I'm in this volunteer group, we do these little art walks, and I used to be more in the middle of planning them. You know, who talks where, what route we take, that sort of thing.

Lately they’ve sort of… quietly moved some of those planning pieces away from me. Nobody made a big announcement or anything. They’re nice people. One of them makes these lemon cookies for meetings—anyway, I can tell they’re trying not to make a thing of it.

And I don’t feel as confident leading the walks as I used to. I still like doing it, but I catch myself wondering if I’m going to miss something or lose track. So yes, I suppose it has caused some problems there.
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or keeping track of the steps in what you need to do?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, organizing things… some things I keep in my head, or I think I do, and then if there are too many parts, I can get a little turned around.

But “often,” I don’t know. My neighbor once showed me this little notebook system he uses—he writes every single errand down, even “buy stamps,” which I thought was funny because who buys stamps anymore? Well, I guess people do.

So… I guess I notice it sometimes, but I’m not sure if it’s more than anyone else. What do you mean by keeping track of steps?
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks?

I don’t know if I’d say “often.” Sometimes I do fine if it’s just one thing, like going to the store—though I still come back with the wrong kind of cereal now and then, but my wife says nobody can read those boxes anymore, they all look the same.

But organizing tasks… I guess if there are several pieces to it, I can lose the thread a little. Not always. It depends what kind of task you mean. Are you talking about chores, or appointments, or bigger things?
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks?

Right, sorry—you did ask that already. I don’t have a clean yes or no. I wouldn’t say I’m a naturally organized person, but I also don’t know if it’s “trouble” in the way you mean.

Like, if someone hands me a form with steps on it, I can usually get through it, though I may need to look back at it a few times. My wife is much better with that sort of thing—she has folders for things, little labels, all of that. I start doing that and then I spend ten minutes deciding what the label should say.

So… maybe sometimes, but I’m not sure I’d call it often. I think I need an example of what kind of task you mean.
Do you notice these attention problems in more than one part of your life, like both at home and outside the home?

I’m not sure. At home is where I notice things more, I guess, because there’s always little stuff sitting around that reminds you you didn’t finish something.

Outside the home… I don’t know. I’m not working now, so there isn’t really an office or anything to compare it to. If I’m at the store or at an appointment, I usually just try to keep it simple. Though stores are terrible now—everything’s moved around, and you go in for one thing and they’ve put it on the other side like it’s a scavenger hunt.

So, I guess I can’t really say clearly if it’s in more than one place. I notice it some at home, but outside the home I’m not sure.
Do you notice the same attention problems when you’re at home?

Yes, at home I do notice it some. Like if I sit down with one of those gallery packets, or even just a set of notes, I start out thinking, “Okay, I’ll read through this,” and for the first few minutes I’m fine.

Then I realize my eyes are still moving across the page, but I’m not really taking any of it in. My mind’s gone somewhere else, and I have to go back and read the same paragraph again. Sometimes more than once. It’s not every single time, but it does happen at home.
Do you often misplace things you need, like keys, glasses, papers, or your phone?

Yeah… that one, yes, I do that. Not so much keys—well, sometimes—but more the odd little things I need for something.

Like I’ll put the camera battery down, or the name tags, or an envelope with the sign-up sheets, and I’ll think, “I’ll put it somewhere safe so I don’t lose it.” And then of course I can’t remember where “safe” was. Then I’m walking around retracing what I did, checking the same table twice, looking under papers… half the morning can go that way.

It’s frustrating, because it’s usually not even gone, it’s just wherever I decided made perfect sense at the time.
Do you often start tasks but not finish them, even when you mean to?

Yes, I do that sometimes. Like with the volunteer group, if somebody gives me a few things to take care of, I’ll get going on the first part—say, printing the maps or something—and that part gets done.

But then there’s another piece, like I was supposed to call the museum desk, or put the folders together, and somehow that just… doesn’t get finished. I’ll leave the folders half-ready on the table, thinking I’m coming right back to them, and then I’m off doing something else.

It’s funny, those folders always take longer than you think anyway, because someone wants the labels a certain way, and then the copier jams—well, not always, but you know. Anyway, yes, I can start it meaning to finish, and then someone has to remind me about the rest.
Do you often forget to do everyday things, like returning a call, paying a bill, or keeping an appointment?

I’m not sure I’d say that’s a big one for me. I mean, appointments I usually put on the calendar, and bills… my wife and I have a little system, so they don’t usually just disappear on me.

Returning calls, maybe sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s forgetting or just not getting around to it right away. And then later I think, “Oh, I should call them,” but by then it’s dinner or the news is on, and—well, that happens to everybody, doesn’t it?

So… I wouldn’t say I’ve really noticed it as a regular problem, no.
Since childhood, have these kinds of attention problems been present most of the time?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, going way back, even in grade school my report cards had those little comments—“daydreams,” or “needs reminders to finish work,” that sort of thing.

My mother used to sit next to me when I was doing homework, before I was twelve anyway, just to keep me moving along. I’d be there with the pencil in my hand and somehow be staring out the window instead. We had this maple tree outside—well, that’s not really the point—but yes, it was there pretty early on, not just something that started recently.
Do you often feel restless, like it’s hard to sit still?

I don’t know that I’d call it restless, exactly. I mean, I can sit, but sometimes I shift around a bit—then again, at my age your back or knee starts talking to you, so it’s hard to know what counts.

Like if I’m watching something, I might get up for tea or to check on something in the kitchen, but I don’t think of it as “I can’t sit still.” I guess I haven’t really noticed that as a main problem. What do you mean by restless, exactly?
Do you often avoid tasks that take a lot of mental effort for a long time, like paperwork or reading long instructions?

Yes, I suppose I do. If it’s something where I have to sit and really read through a long description—like at a museum, those exhibit plaques, or even planning out something I’m supposed to say—I’ll suddenly remember the laundry needs moving, or the mail needs sorting.

It’s not that I refuse to do it, exactly. It just feels like… pulling teeth to stay with all that reading or organizing in my head, so I keep doing little chores first. Then, of course, half the morning’s gone.
Besides at home and with the museum group, did you have the same kind of attention problems in a job or at school?

School, definitely. I mean, I didn’t go far with school, just high school, but even back in grade school it was there. The report cards would have those comments like “daydreams” or “needs reminders to finish work.”

And my mother—she was very patient, really—she used to sit beside me while I did homework, before I was twelve, just to keep me moving along. Otherwise I’d sort of drift off. So yes, at school, anyway. Jobs… I’m not really thinking of a clear example right now.

doctor.question: Do you often misplace things you need, like keys, glasses, papers, or your phone?

target_item.name: Losing_Items
target_item.manifestation: I’m always putting down the camera battery, name tags, or the envelope with sign-up sheets somewhere safe and then spending half the morning retracing my steps to find them.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about often misplacing needed items such as keys, glasses, papers, or phone, which directly matches losing things necessary for tasks or activities.

patient.answer:
Yeah… that one, yes, I do that. Not so much keys—well, sometimes—but more the odd little things I need for something.

Like I’ll put the camera battery down, or the name tags, or an envelope with the sign-up sheets, and I’ll think, “I’ll put it somewhere safe so I don’t lose it.” And then of course I can’t remember where “safe” was. Then I’m walking around retracing what I did, checking the same table twice, looking under papers… half the morning can go that way.

It’s frustrating, because it’s usually not even gone, it’s just wherever I decided made perfect sense at the time.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD, predominantly inattentive type from a nonspecific concentration problem by checking for a core ADHD symptom the patient has not yet clearly endorsed: failure to follow through on tasks.
doctor.question: Do you often start tasks but not finish them, even when you mean to?

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When someone gives me a few things to handle for the volunteer group, I’ll do the first part, like printing the maps, but then I may forget to call the museum desk or leave the folders half-ready until someone reminds me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about starting tasks but not completing them, which directly matches difficulty following through and finishing duties or tasks.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do that sometimes. Like with the volunteer group, if somebody gives me a few things to take care of, I’ll get going on the first part—say, printing the maps or something—and that part gets done.

But then there’s another piece, like I was supposed to call the museum desk, or put the folders together, and somehow that just… doesn’t get finished. I’ll leave the folders half-ready on the table, thinking I’m coming right back to them, and then I’m off doing something else.

It’s funny, those folders always take longer than you think anyway, because someone wants the labels a certain way, and then the copier jams—well, not always, but you know. Anyway, yes, I can start it meaning to finish, and then someone has to remind me about the rest.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ADHD predominantly inattentive type from nonspecific attention/concentration problems by testing for another core inattentive symptom: forgetfulness in daily activities.
doctor.question: Do you often forget to do everyday things, like returning a call, paying a bill, or keeping an appointment?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about being forgetful in everyday activities, such as returning calls, paying bills, or keeping appointments. That symptom is not directly covered in the provided profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say that’s a big one for me. I mean, appointments I usually put on the calendar, and bills… my wife and I have a little system, so they don’t usually just disappear on me.

Returning calls, maybe sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s forgetting or just not getting around to it right away. And then later I think, “Oh, I should call them,” but by then it’s dinner or the news is on, and—well, that happens to everybody, doesn’t it?

So… I wouldn’t say I’ve really noticed it as a regular problem, no.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms have been persistent since childhood rather than representing nonspecific attention difficulty, which helps distinguish ADHD predominantly inattentive presentation from unspecified attention/concentration problems.
doctor.question: Since childhood, have these kinds of attention problems been present most of the time?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even back in grade school, my report cards said things like “daydreams” and “needs reminders to finish work,” and my mother used to sit beside me to keep me on track with homework before I was twelve.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the attention problems have been present since childhood, which directly corresponds to onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think so. I mean, going way back, even in grade school my report cards had those little comments—“daydreams,” or “needs reminders to finish work,” that sort of thing.

My mother used to sit next to me when I was doing homework, before I was twelve anyway, just to keep me moving along. I’d be there with the pencil in my hand and somehow be staring out the window instead. We had this maple tree outside—well, that’s not really the point—but yes, it was there pretty early on, not just something that started recently.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient also shows hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, which would separate ADHD predominantly inattentive type from nonspecific attention/concentration problems.
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless, like it’s hard to sit still?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about restlessness or difficulty sitting still, which is a hyperactivity symptom and is not covered by the provided inattentive symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d call it restless, exactly. I mean, I can sit, but sometimes I shift around a bit—then again, at my age your back or knee starts talking to you, so it’s hard to know what counts.

Like if I’m watching something, I might get up for tea or to check on something in the kitchen, but I don’t think of it as “I can’t sit still.” I guess I haven’t really noticed that as a main problem. What do you mean by restless, exactly?

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are enough additional inattentive ADHD symptoms beyond concentration lapses to distinguish ADHD predominantly inattentive presentation from nonspecific attention/concentration difficulty.
doctor.question: Do you often avoid tasks that take a lot of mental effort for a long time, like paperwork or reading long instructions?

target_item.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: If I know I need to read through a long exhibit description or plan out a talk, I keep finding little chores around the house to do first because sitting with all that reading feels like pulling teeth.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding long, mentally demanding tasks such as paperwork or reading instructions, which directly matches sustained mental effort avoidance.

patient.answer:
Yes, I suppose I do. If it’s something where I have to sit and really read through a long description—like at a museum, those exhibit plaques, or even planning out something I’m supposed to say—I’ll suddenly remember the laundry needs moving, or the mail needs sorting.

It’s not that I refuse to do it, exactly. It just feels like… pulling teeth to stay with all that reading or organizing in my head, so I keep doing little chores first. Then, of course, half the morning’s gone.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention problems occur in at least two settings, which is needed to distinguish ADHD predominantly inattentive type from isolated concentration difficulty.
doctor.question: Besides at home and with the museum group, did you have the same kind of attention problems in a job or at school?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even back in grade school, my report cards said things like “daydreams” and “needs reminders to finish work,” and my mother used to sit beside me to keep me on track with homework before I was twelve.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the attention problems also occurred in another setting such as school or work; the available profile item that covers school-related attention problems is the childhood school history before age 12.

patient.answer:
School, definitely. I mean, I didn’t go far with school, just high school, but even back in grade school it was there. The report cards would have those comments like “daydreams” or “needs reminders to finish work.”

And my mother—she was very patient, really—she used to sit beside me while I did homework, before I was twelve, just to keep me moving along. Otherwise I’d sort of drift off. So yes, at school, anyway. Jobs… I’m not really thinking of a clear example right now.

inference.note: Narrowed to F90.0. The patient endorses a persistent inattentive pattern since childhood (<12), across settings (school, home, volunteer role), with functional impairment and multiple inattentive symptoms (poor sustained attention/listening, losing things, unfinished tasks, avoiding sustained mental effort). Auditory-processing concern is not supported, so R41.840 is ruled out as the primary candidate.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation: longstanding inattentive symptoms since childhood, present across school/home/community volunteer settings, with clear functional impact. The patient endorsed multiple core inattention symptoms including failing to sustain attention in conversation and reading, not seeming to register spoken information, misplacing necessary items, leaving tasks unfinished, avoiding sustained mental effort, and childhood history of daydreaming/need for reminders before age 12. Depression, anxiety, and primary hearing/language-auditory problems were not supported as better explanations in the interview.
